steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for our paper on a joint control variate for black-box variational inference. Explain why gradient variance is a problem in BBVI, why existing variance reduction and incremental gradient methods each handle only one noise source, and summarize our method and results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. BBVI as an alternative to MCMC
2. Doubly-stochastic gradients and their variance
3. Existing Monte Carlo variance reduction and its limits
4. Incremental gradient methods and their limits
5. Our method: joint control of both noise sources

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. BBVI
- popular alternative to MCMC
- posit variational family, optimize to be close to posterior; only black-box evaluations (density or gradient)
- minimize KL-divergence by stochastic optimization with unbiased gradient estimates
- allows data subsampling -> big speed-up on large datasets

2. Doubly-stochastic
- two sources of randomness: Monte Carlo sampling from variational distribution; data subsampling
- high gradient variance -> small stepsizes -> slow convergence

3. Reducing Monte Carlo noise
- many methods: approximation of objective where MC noise integrates exactly
- gives a control variate: zero mean, negatively correlated with original gradient estimator
- with subsampling: separate approximation per datum
- only per-datum MC noise reduced, not subsampling noise
- subsampling noise often dominant (Sec. 3)

4. Incremental gradient methods
- non-BBVI problems with only subsampling noise; 'recycle' previous gradient evaluations
- with few exceptions (Sec. 6) ignore MC noise; rely on running averages -> not usable for doubly-stochastic problems

5. Our method
- jointly controls MC and subsampling noise
- per-datum approximations of the target, MC noise integrated exactly
- running averages of approximate gradients (noise integrated) -> incremental gradient ideas for doubly-stochastic problems
- handles both noises and their interactions
- experiments on a range of probabilistic models: lower variance, much faster convergence

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Black-box variational inference (BBVI) is a popular alternative to Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. The idea is to choose a variational family and optimize it so it is close to the posterior, using only "black-box" evaluations of the target model (either the density or the gradient). This is usually done by minimizing the KL-divergence with stochastic optimization methods that use unbiased gradient estimates. Often this means data subsampling can be used, and this speeds up optimization a lot when datasets are large.

The BBVI optimization problem is often called "doubly-stochastic", because there are two sources of randomness in the gradient estimation: Monte Carlo sampling from the variational distribution, and subsampling data from the full dataset. Because it is doubly-stochastic, a common challenge for BBVI is the variance of the gradient estimates. If the variance is high, small stepsizes have to be used, and optimization converges slowly.

3. Reducing Monte Carlo noise
- many methods: approximation of objective where MC noise integrates exactly
- gives a control variate: zero mean, negatively correlated with original gradient estimator
- with subsampling: separate approximation per datum
- only per-datum MC noise reduced, not subsampling noise
- subsampling noise often dominant (Sec. 3)

4. Incremental gradient methods
- non-BBVI problems with only subsampling noise; 'recycle' previous gradient evaluations
- with few exceptions (Sec. 6) ignore MC noise; rely on running averages -> not usable for doubly-stochastic problems

5. Our method
- jointly controls MC and subsampling noise
- per-datum approximations of the target, MC noise integrated exactly
- running averages of approximate gradients (noise integrated) -> incremental gradient ideas for doubly-stochastic problems
- handles both noises and their interactions
- experiments on a range of probabilistic models: lower variance, much faster convergence

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Black-box variational inference (BBVI) is a popular alternative to Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. The idea is to choose a variational family and optimize it so it is close to the posterior, using only "black-box" evaluations of the target model (either the density or the gradient). This is usually done by minimizing the KL-divergence with stochastic optimization methods that use unbiased gradient estimates. Often this means data subsampling can be used, and this speeds up optimization a lot when datasets are large.

The BBVI optimization problem is often called "doubly-stochastic", because there are two sources of randomness in the gradient estimation: Monte Carlo sampling from the variational distribution, and subsampling data from the full dataset. Because it is doubly-stochastic, a common challenge for BBVI is the variance of the gradient estimates. If the variance is high, small stepsizes have to be used, and optimization converges slowly.

There are many methods to reduce the "Monte Carlo" noise that comes from drawing samples from the variational distribution. Usually these can be seen as building an approximation of the objective where the Monte Carlo noise can be integrated exactly. This approximation can then be used to define a control variate, which is a zero mean random variable that is negatively correlated with the original gradient estimator. Sometimes these methods can be used together with data subsampling, basically by making a different approximation for each datum. But they can only reduce the per-datum Monte Carlo noise, and they do not reduce the subsampling noise itself. This is important, because subsampling noise is often the main source of gradient variance (Sec. 3).

For optimization problems (not BBVI) that only have subsampling noise, there are many incremental gradient methods that "recycle" earlier gradient evaluations to speed up convergence. But with few exceptions (Sec. 6) these methods do not deal with Monte Carlo noise, and since they rely on efficiently keeping running averages, they cannot be applied to doubly-stochastic problems.

In this paper we present a method that controls Monte Carlo noise and subsampling noise jointly. The idea is to make approximations of the target for each datum where the Monte Carlo noise can be integrated exactly. The method keeps running averages of the approximate gradients with the noise integrated, and this gets around the problem of applying incremental gradient ideas to doubly-stochastic problems. The method deals with both kinds of noise and also with the interactions between them. Experiments with variational inference on a range of probabilistic models show that the method gives lower variance gradients and much faster convergence than existing approaches.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Black-box variational inference (BBVI) [1,2,3,4,5] is a popular alternative to Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. The idea is to posit a variational family and optimize it to be close to the posterior, using only "black-box" evaluations of the target model (either the density or the gradient). This is typically done by minimizing the KL-divergence with stochastic optimization methods using unbiased gradient estimates. Often, this allows data subsampling, which greatly speeds up optimization on large datasets.

The BBVI optimization problem is often called "doubly-stochastic" [2,6], since gradient estimation has two sources of randomness: Monte Carlo sampling from the variational distribution, and data subsampling from the full dataset. Because of this doubly-stochastic nature, a common challenge for BBVI is the variance of the gradient estimates: if it is high, small stepsizes are needed, leading to slow optimization convergence [7,8].

Numerous methods exist to reduce the "Monte Carlo" noise that comes from drawing samples from the variational distribution [9,10,11,12,13]. These can typically be seen as building an approximation of the objective for which the Monte Carlo noise can be integrated exactly. This approximation can then define a control variate—a zero mean random variable negatively correlated with the original gradient estimator. These methods can sometimes be combined with data subsampling, essentially by creating a different approximation for each datum. However, they can only reduce per-datum Monte Carlo noise; they do not reduce the subsampling noise itself. This is critical, since subsampling noise is often the dominant source of gradient variance (Sec. 3).

For (non-BBVI) optimization problems with only subsampling noise, there are numerous incremental gradient methods that "recycle" previous gradient evaluations to speed up convergence [14,15,16,17,18]. However, with few exceptions (Sec. 6), these methods do not address Monte Carlo noise and, because they rely on efficiently maintaining running averages, cannot be applied to doubly-stochastic problems.

This paper presents a method that jointly controls Monte Carlo and subsampling noise. The idea is to create approximations of the target for each datum, for which the Monte Carlo noise can be integrated exactly. The method maintains running averages of the approximate gradients, with the noise integrated, which overcomes the challenge of applying incremental gradient ideas to doubly-stochastic problems. It addresses both forms of noise as well as the interactions between them. Experiments with variational inference on a range of probabilistic models show that the method yields lower variance gradients and significantly faster convergence than existing approaches.
